items.stem: What does a production possibility curve show?
options: The combinations of two goods consumers want
The actual output of an economy each year
The maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with all its resources fully and efficiently employed
items.answer: The maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with all its resources fully and efficiently employed
items.markingKey: PPC: maximum output combinations given resources and technology.

items.stem: Explain why a PPC is usually concave to the origin.
items.answer: Resources are specialised and not equally efficient in producing both goods. As more of one good is produced, resources less suited to it must be used, so increasing amounts of the other good are given up.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: resources not equally suited; 1 mark: increasing opportunity cost; 1 mark: link to shape [3]

items.stem: Explain under what conditions a PPC would be a straight line.
items.answer: If resources are equally productive in both uses, each extra unit of one good always costs the same amount of the other, giving constant opportunity cost.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: resources equally suited; 1 mark: constant opportunity cost [2]

items.stem: The table shows the production possibilities of Merania. Combination: A, B, C, D, E; healthcare (units): 0, 10, 20, 30, 40; education (units): 300, 280, 220, 120, 0. Calculate the opportunity cost of one unit of healthcare when moving from D to E.
items.answer: 12 units of education
items.markingKey: Δeducation = 120, Δhealthcare = 10; 120/10 = 12.

items.stem: The table shows the production possibilities of Jovania. Combination: A, B, C, D, E; agricultural goods (units): 0, 10, 20, 30, 40; industrial goods (units): 140, 130, 100, 60, 0. (a) Calculate the opportunity cost of one unit of agricultural goods for each move from A to E. (b) State whether opportunity cost is constant or increasing and describe the shape of the PPC. (c) Explain why it has this shape.
items.answer: (a) 1, 3, 4, 6 units of industrial goods per unit of agricultural goods. (b) Increasing opportunity cost; concave (bowed outwards) PPC. (c) Resources are not equally suited to both goods, so increasingly unsuitable resources are moved.
items.markingKey: (a) all four values [2] (b) shape [1] (c) reason [1] [4]

items.stem: The table shows the production possibilities of Westaria. Combination: A, B, C, D, E; wheat (units): 0, 20, 40, 60, 80; cars (units): 100, 90, 70, 40, 0. (a) Calculate the opportunity cost of one unit of wheat for each move from A to E. (b) State whether opportunity cost is constant or increasing and describe the shape of the PPC. (c) Explain why it has this shape.
items.answer: (a) 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2 units of cars per unit of wheat. (b) Increasing opportunity cost; concave (bowed outwards) PPC. (c) Resources are not equally suited to both goods, so increasingly unsuitable resources are moved.
items.markingKey: (a) all four values [2] (b) shape [1] (c) reason [1] [4]

items.stem: Extract: During a recession unemployment in Jovania rose from 6% to 13%. The government responded with a programme to build new ports and railways, raising investment to 25% of GDP. Critics argue that the programme diverts resources away from consumer goods. At the same time a drought reduced the area of farmland that could be used. (a) Explain the opportunity cost of the investment programme once the economy returns to full employment. (b) Explain the effect of the drought on the PPC.
items.answer: (a) Moving along the PPC: more capital goods means fewer consumer goods now. (b) Loss of land reduces capacity (especially for food) so the PPC shifts or pivots inwards.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Moving along the PPC: more capital goods means fewer consumer goods now. [2] (b) Credit: Loss of land reduces capacity (especially for food) so the PPC shifts or pivots inwards. [2]

items.stem: Extract: During a recession unemployment in Quentara rose from 5% to 11%. The government responded with a programme to build new ports and railways, raising investment to 15% of GDP. Critics argue that the programme diverts resources away from consumer goods. At the same time a drought reduced the area of farmland that could be used. (a) Calculate the change in unemployment in percentage points. (b) Using a PPC, explain how the recession would be shown. (c) Explain the opportunity cost of the investment programme once the economy returns to full employment.
items.answer: (a) 6 percentage points (b) A movement to a point inside the PPC: resources idle, capacity unchanged. (c) Moving along the PPC: more capital goods means fewer consumer goods now.
items.markingKey: (a) 11 − 5 [1] (b) Credit: A movement to a point inside the PPC: resources idle, capacity unchanged. [2] (c) Credit: Moving along the PPC: more capital goods means fewer consumer goods now. [2]

items.stem: Why is a PPC usually drawn concave (bowed outwards) to the origin?
options: Resources are not equally suited to producing both goods, so opportunity cost increases
Resources are equally suited to both goods
items.answer: Resources are not equally suited to producing both goods, so opportunity cost increases
items.markingKey: Increasing opportunity cost: moving resources less suited to the other good.

items.stem: Explain how a PPC illustrates the concepts of scarcity, choice and opportunity cost.
items.answer: Scarcity: points beyond the curve are unattainable. Choice: the economy must choose a point on the curve. Opportunity cost: moving along it means giving up some of one good to get more of the other.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each concept linked to the PPC [3]

items.stem: Istrana moves resources from producing textiles to producing car tyres. Using a PPC, explain why the opportunity cost of extra car tyres rises as more is produced.
items.answer: Workers and machines best suited to car tyres move first; later the resources moved are less suited, so more textiles must be given up for each extra unit of car tyres: a concave PPC.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: resources not equally suited; 1 mark: rising sacrifice/concave PPC [2]

items.stem: The table shows the production possibilities of Halvoria. Combination: A, B, C, D, E; food (units): 0, 100, 200, 300, 400; manufactured goods (units): 900, 750, 550, 300, 0. Calculate the opportunity cost of one unit of food when moving from D to E.
items.answer: 3 units of manufactured goods
items.markingKey: Δmanufactured goods = 300, Δfood = 100; 300/100 = 3.

items.stem: Newspapers in Valdoria have recently reported a lively debate among economists on this issue. With the help of a PPC diagram, explain the difference between constant and increasing opportunity cost.
items.answer: Straight-line PPC: resources equally suited, constant slope; concave PPC: resources specialised, slope steepens; example of moving resources; axes labelled with the two goods.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Straight-line PPC: resources equally suited, constant slope; concave PPC: resources specialised, slope steepens; example of moving resources; axes labelled with the two goods. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: Extract: During a recession unemployment in Westaria rose from 4% to 9%. The government responded with a programme to build new ports and railways, raising investment to 15% of GDP. Critics argue that the programme diverts resources away from consumer goods. At the same time a drought reduced the area of farmland that could be used. (a) Explain the opportunity cost of the investment programme once the economy returns to full employment. (b) Explain the effect of the drought on the PPC.
items.answer: (a) Moving along the PPC: more capital goods means fewer consumer goods now. (b) Loss of land reduces capacity (especially for food) so the PPC shifts or pivots inwards.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Moving along the PPC: more capital goods means fewer consumer goods now. [2] (b) Credit: Loss of land reduces capacity (especially for food) so the PPC shifts or pivots inwards. [2]

items.stem: A policy institute in Bangkok has published a report on this issue for the government of Umbria Nova. ‘The PPC is a useful model for explaining the choices facing Umbria Nova.’ Evaluate this view.
items.answer: For: Illustrates scarcity, choice, opportunity cost, efficiency, unemployment and growth clearly. Against: Only two goods; assumes fixed resources and technology; opportunity cost hard to measure; ignores distribution and consumer preferences; still a helpful simplification. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement on when the claim holds.
items.markingKey: Analysis (AO1/AO2, up to 8): Illustrates scarcity, choice, opportunity cost, efficiency, unemployment and growth clearly. Evaluation (AO3, up to 4): Only two goods; assumes fixed resources and technology; opportunity cost hard to measure; ignores distribution and consumer preferences; still a helpful simplification. Top marks need balanced analysis of both sides and a justified conclusion that answers the question set, explaining what the outcome depends on [12]

items.stem: What does a point inside a PPC show?
options: Some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently
An output that cannot be reached
The economy is producing at full capacity
items.answer: Some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently
items.markingKey: Inside: under-utilisation; output could rise without giving up anything.

items.stem: Explain why a recession might be shown by a point inside a PPC.
items.answer: In a recession output falls and workers and machines are unemployed, so the economy produces less than it could; it is inside the curve.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: unemployed resources; 1 mark: output below potential [2]

items.stem: Explain why moving from inside the PPC to the curve has no opportunity cost.
items.answer: The extra output comes from previously unused resources, so no production of the other good has to be given up.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: idle resources used; 1 mark: nothing given up [2]

items.stem: The table shows the maximum combinations of healthcare and education that Korvia can produce. Combination: A, B, C, D, E; healthcare: 0, 50, 100, 150, 200; education: 400, 350, 275, 150, 0. Korvia is currently producing 100 units of healthcare and 275 units of education. Which describes this position?
options: On the PPC: the economy is experiencing economic growth
On the PPC: resources fully and efficiently employed
Inside the PPC: some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently
Beyond the PPC: unattainable with current resources and technology
items.answer: On the PPC: resources fully and efficiently employed
items.markingKey: At 100 units of healthcare the maximum of education is 275; 275 is equal to this.

items.stem: The table shows the maximum combinations of healthcare and education that Valdoria can produce. Combination: A, B, C, D, E; healthcare: 0, 50, 100, 150, 200; education: 280, 260, 220, 120, 0. Valdoria is currently producing 100 units of healthcare and 180 units of education. (a) Explain whether this output is efficient. (b) Calculate the extra education that could be produced without giving up any healthcare. (c) Explain one reason why an economy might be at this point.
items.answer: (a) Inside the PPC: some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently. (b) 40 units. (c) Unemployment, e.g. a recession, or inefficient use of resources.
items.markingKey: (a) compare with maximum 220 [1]; conclusion [1] (b) 220 − 180 = 40 [1] (c) reason [1] [4]

items.stem: Extract: During a recession unemployment in Quentara rose from 5% to 11%. The government responded with a programme to build new ports and railways, raising investment to 20% of GDP. Critics argue that the programme diverts resources away from consumer goods. At the same time a drought reduced the area of farmland that could be used. (a) Using a PPC, explain how the recession would be shown. (b) Explain the effect of the drought on the PPC.
items.answer: (a) A movement to a point inside the PPC: resources idle, capacity unchanged. (b) Loss of land reduces capacity (especially for food) so the PPC shifts or pivots inwards.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: A movement to a point inside the PPC: resources idle, capacity unchanged. [2] (b) Credit: Loss of land reduces capacity (especially for food) so the PPC shifts or pivots inwards. [2]

items.stem: What does a point beyond the PPC show?
options: An output combination that is unattainable with current resources and technology
items.answer: An output combination that is unattainable with current resources and technology
items.markingKey: Beyond: unattainable (in the absence of trade or growth).

items.stem: Explain how international trade could allow a country to consume at a point beyond its PPC.
items.answer: By specialising according to comparative advantage and trading, the country can import goods at a lower opportunity cost than producing them, so consumption exceeds what it could produce alone.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: specialisation and trade; 1 mark: consumption beyond production possibilities [2]

items.stem: The table shows the maximum combinations of agricultural goods and industrial goods that Korvia can produce. Combination: A, B, C, D, E; agricultural goods: 0, 20, 40, 60, 80; industrial goods: 280, 260, 220, 120, 0. Korvia is currently producing 20 units of agricultural goods and 300 units of industrial goods. Which describes this position?
options: On the PPC: the economy is experiencing economic growth
Beyond the PPC: unattainable with current resources and technology
Inside the PPC: some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently
On the PPC: resources fully and efficiently employed
items.answer: Beyond the PPC: unattainable with current resources and technology
items.markingKey: At 20 units of agricultural goods the maximum of industrial goods is 260; 300 is more than this.

items.stem: The table shows the maximum combinations of consumer goods and capital goods that Westaria can produce. Combination: A, B, C, D, E; consumer goods: 0, 20, 40, 60, 80; capital goods: 350, 325, 250, 150, 0. Westaria is currently producing 40 units of consumer goods and 250 units of capital goods. (a) Explain whether this output is efficient. (b) Calculate the extra capital goods that could be produced without giving up any consumer goods. (c) Explain one reason why an economy might be at this point.
items.answer: (a) On the PPC: resources fully and efficiently employed. (b) 0 units. (c) Not applicable: it is already on the PPC, so more requires giving up some consumer goods.
items.markingKey: (a) compare with maximum 250 [1]; conclusion [1] (b) 250 − 250 = 0 [1] (c) reason [1] [4]

items.stem: Which would shift a country’s PPC outwards?
options: A rise in the price level
A movement of workers from farming to manufacturing
items.answer: An improvement in technology
items.markingKey: Outward shift: more/better resources or technology.

items.stem: Explain two causes of an outward shift of a country’s PPC.
items.answer: An increase in the quantity of resources (e.g. labour force growth, discovery of minerals, investment in capital); an improvement in quality (education, training) or technology.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each cause, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: Explain why a country that chooses to produce more capital goods and fewer consumer goods now may enjoy higher living standards in future.
items.answer: Today’s opportunity cost is fewer consumer goods, but more capital raises productive capacity, shifting the PPC outwards, so more of both can be produced later.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: opportunity cost now; 1 mark: capital raises capacity/PPC shifts out; 1 mark: more consumption later [3]

items.stem: Fendaria discovers large new reserves of natural gas. How would this be shown on the country’s PPC?
options: Outward pivot of the PPC on the food axis
Movement from inside towards the PPC
items.answer: Outward shift of the PPC
items.markingKey: Outward shift of the PPC: more natural resources raise productive capacity.

items.stem: Ostrelia moves workers from farming into building houses. How would this be shown on the country’s PPC? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Movement along the PPC: existing resources are reallocated between goods.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Movement along the PPC; 1 mark: explanation – existing resources are reallocated between goods. [2]

items.stem: Explain, with the help of a diagram, the factors that could cause a country’s PPC to shift outwards.
items.answer: More or better resources: labour force growth, education, investment in capital, discovery of resources, technology; parallel shift vs pivot.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: More or better resources: labour force growth, education, investment in capital, discovery of resources, technology; parallel shift vs pivot. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: Explain the difference between a movement along a PPC and a shift of a PPC.
items.answer: A movement along shows a reallocation of existing resources between the two goods; a shift shows a change in the total productive capacity (quantity/quality of resources or technology).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: movement = reallocation; 1 mark: shift = change in capacity [2]

items.stem: Climate change is causing desertification of farmland in Umbria Nova. Explain the likely effect on Umbria Nova’s PPC.
items.answer: Less usable land reduces productive capacity, especially for food, so the PPC shifts (or pivots) inwards.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: loss of land resource; 1 mark: inward shift/pivot [2]

items.stem: Before a change, Ostrelia could produce a maximum of 80 units of wheat or 240 units of cars. After a rise in the size and skills of its labour force, the maximum output of wheat rose by 10% and that of cars by 10%. Calculate the new maximum output of wheat.
items.answer: 88 units

items.stem: For each event, state how it would be shown on a PPC and explain why. (i) Many young skilled workers emigrate from Halvoria. (ii) Halvoria moves workers from farming into building houses. (iii) A new irrigation technology raises crop yields in Halvoria but has no effect on manufacturing.
items.answer: (i) Inward shift of the PPC (ii) Movement along the PPC (iii) Outward pivot of the PPC on the food axis
items.markingKey: (i) Inward shift of the PPC – the quantity and quality of labour fall. [2] (ii) Movement along the PPC – existing resources are reallocated between goods. [2] (iii) Outward pivot of the PPC on the food axis – only the maximum output of food rises. [2] Total [6]

items.stem: What does a straight-line PPC indicate?
items.answer: Constant opportunity cost
items.markingKey: A constant slope means the same amount of Y is given up for each extra unit of X.

items.stem: Pelora moves resources from producing chocolate bars to producing bicycles. Using a PPC, explain why the opportunity cost of extra bicycles rises as more is produced.
items.answer: Workers and machines best suited to bicycles move first; later the resources moved are less suited, so more chocolate bars must be given up for each extra unit of bicycles: a concave PPC.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: resources not equally suited; 1 mark: rising sacrifice/concave PPC [2]

items.stem: Selmaria moves resources from producing textiles to producing electric scooters. Using a PPC, explain why the opportunity cost of extra electric scooters rises as more is produced.
items.answer: Workers and machines best suited to electric scooters move first; later the resources moved are less suited, so more textiles must be given up for each extra unit of electric scooters: a concave PPC.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: resources not equally suited; 1 mark: rising sacrifice/concave PPC [2]

items.stem: The table shows the production possibilities of Zentara. Combination: A, B, C, D, E; agricultural goods (units): 0, 10, 20, 30, 40; industrial goods (units): 120, 110, 90, 60, 0. Calculate the opportunity cost of one unit of agricultural goods when moving from C to D.
items.answer: 3 units of industrial goods
items.markingKey: Δindustrial goods = 30, Δagricultural goods = 10; 30/10 = 3.

items.stem: The table shows the production possibilities of Selmaria. Combination: A, B, C, D, E; healthcare (units): 0, 10, 20, 30, 40; education (units): 350, 300, 225, 125, 0. Calculate the opportunity cost of one unit of healthcare when moving from D to E.
items.answer: 12.5 units of education
items.markingKey: Δeducation = 125, Δhealthcare = 10; 125/10 = 12.5.

items.stem: The table shows the production possibilities of Fendaria. Combination: A, B, C, D, E; food (units): 0, 100, 200, 300, 400; manufactured goods (units): 260, 240, 200, 120, 0. Calculate the opportunity cost of one unit of food when moving from C to D.
items.answer: 0.8 units of manufactured goods
items.markingKey: Δmanufactured goods = 80, Δfood = 100; 80/100 = 0.8.

items.answer: Straight-line PPC: resources equally suited, constant slope; concave PPC: resources specialised, slope steepens; example of moving resources; axes labelled with the two goods.

items.stem: Why do all points on the PPC represent productive efficiency?
options: Prices are equal at each point
Consumers are equally happy at each point
Every point gives the same total output
More of one good cannot be produced without producing less of the other
items.answer: More of one good cannot be produced without producing less of the other
items.markingKey: On the curve: resources fully and efficiently used.

items.stem: Strikes have closed many factories in Merania for three months. Explain the effect on Merania’s position relative to its PPC.
items.answer: Output falls below potential while workers and machines are idle, so the economy moves to a point inside the PPC; the PPC itself does not shift.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: moves inside; 1 mark: PPC unchanged/capacity not destroyed [2]

items.stem: Unemployment in Quentara has risen to 12%. Explain how this would be shown on Quentara’s PPC.
items.answer: A point inside the PPC: resources (labour) are idle, so actual output is below the maximum possible.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: inside the PPC; 1 mark: idle resources explained [2]

items.stem: The table shows the maximum combinations of consumer goods and capital goods that Loristan can produce. Combination: A, B, C, D, E; consumer goods: 0, 20, 40, 60, 80; capital goods: 350, 300, 225, 125, 0. Loristan is currently producing 40 units of consumer goods and 275 units of capital goods. Which describes this position?
options: Beyond the PPC: unattainable with current resources and technology
Inside the PPC: some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently
On the PPC: resources fully and efficiently employed
On the PPC: the economy is experiencing economic growth
items.answer: Beyond the PPC: unattainable with current resources and technology
items.markingKey: At 40 units of consumer goods the maximum of capital goods is 225; 275 is more than this.

(a) Explain whether this output is efficient. (b) Calculate the extra manufactured goods that could be produced without giving up any food. (c) Explain one reason why an economy might be at this point.
items.answer: (a) Inside the PPC: some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently. (b) 20 units. (c) Unemployment, e.g. a recession, or inefficient use of resources.
items.markingKey: (a) compare with maximum 90 [1]; conclusion [1] (b) 90 − 70 = 20 [1] (c) reason [1] [4]

items.stem: Which would shift a country’s PPC inwards?
options: A natural disaster that destroys factories and farmland
items.answer: A natural disaster that destroys factories and farmland
items.markingKey: Loss of resources reduces productive capacity.

items.stem: During a class discussion Leila said: ‘A fall in unemployment causes the PPC to shift outwards.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: A fall in unemployment moves the economy from inside towards the PPC; the PPC shifts only when capacity changes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – A fall in unemployment moves the economy from inside towards the PPC; the PPC shifts only when capacity changes. [2]

items.stem: Kestria invests heavily in robots for its factories. Explain the effect on its PPC for agricultural and manufactured goods.
items.answer: Productive capacity in manufacturing rises, so the PPC pivots outwards along the manufactured goods axis; capacity in agriculture is unchanged.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: capacity in manufacturing; 1 mark: pivot not parallel shift [2]

items.stem: Quentara moves workers from farming into building houses. How would this be shown on the country’s PPC?
options: Outward pivot of the PPC on the food axis
Movement from inside towards the PPC
items.answer: Movement along the PPC
items.markingKey: Movement along the PPC: existing resources are reallocated between goods.

items.stem: Before a change, Calvania could produce a maximum of 150 units of consumer goods or 300 units of capital goods. After a new technology used only in producing consumer goods, the maximum output of consumer goods rose by 20% while the maximum output of capital goods was unchanged. (a) Calculate the new maximum outputs of consumer goods and capital goods. (b) Describe how the PPC has changed. (c) Explain what happens to the opportunity cost of consumer goods in terms of capital goods (assume a straight-line PPC).
items.answer: (a) 180 consumer goods; 300 capital goods. (b) Outward pivot along the consumer goods axis. (c) Before: 2 capital goods per consumer goods; after: 1.67: it falls, because producing consumer goods is now more efficient.
items.markingKey: (a) both maxima [2] (b) shift/pivot [1] (c) both opportunity costs and conclusion [2] [5]

items.stem: What does the slope of a PPC measure?
options: The opportunity cost of one good in terms of the other
items.answer: The opportunity cost of one good in terms of the other
items.markingKey: Slope = ΔY/ΔX = units of Y forgone per unit of X.

items.stem: During a class discussion Sipho said: ‘The PPC shows the combinations of goods that consumers want to buy.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: It shows the maximum combinations an economy can produce with its resources and technology, not consumer preferences.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – It shows the maximum combinations an economy can produce with its resources and technology, not consumer preferences. [2]

items.stem: Daniel makes the following statement: ‘The PPC shows the combinations of goods that consumers want to buy.’ Explain what is wrong with this claim.
items.answer: It shows the maximum combinations an economy can produce with its resources and technology, not consumer preferences.

items.answer: 2 units of cars

items.stem: The table shows the production possibilities of Ostrelia. Combination: A, B, C, D, E; wheat (units): 0, 100, 200, 300, 400; cars (units): 800, 750, 550, 300, 0. Calculate the opportunity cost of one unit of wheat when moving from C to D.
items.answer: 2.5 units of cars

items.stem: The table shows the production possibilities of Lunaria. Combination: A, B, C, D, E; food (units): 0, 20, 40, 60, 80; manufactured goods (units): 320, 300, 220, 120, 0. Calculate the opportunity cost of one unit of food when moving from D to E.
items.answer: 6 units of manufactured goods
items.markingKey: Δmanufactured goods = 120, Δfood = 20; 120/20 = 6.

items.stem: The government of Loristan has asked its economic advisers for a report on this issue. With the help of a PPC diagram, explain the difference between constant and increasing opportunity cost.
items.answer: Straight-line PPC: resources equally suited, constant slope; concave PPC: resources specialised, slope steepens; example of moving resources; axes labelled with the two goods.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Straight-line PPC: resources equally suited, constant slope; concave PPC: resources specialised, slope steepens; example of moving resources; axes labelled with the two goods. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: Extract: During a recession unemployment in Quentara rose from 4% to 9%. The government responded with a programme to build new ports and railways, raising investment to 15% of GDP. Critics argue that the programme diverts resources away from consumer goods. At the same time a drought reduced the area of farmland that could be used. (a) Using a PPC, explain how the recession would be shown. (b) Explain the effect of the drought on the PPC.
items.answer: (a) A movement to a point inside the PPC: resources idle, capacity unchanged. (b) Loss of land reduces capacity (especially for food) so the PPC shifts or pivots inwards.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: A movement to a point inside the PPC: resources idle, capacity unchanged. [2] (b) Credit: Loss of land reduces capacity (especially for food) so the PPC shifts or pivots inwards. [2]

items.stem: A movement from a point inside the PPC to a point on it, during a recovery, shows
options: a fall in unemployment of resources
an outward shift of the PPC
items.answer: a fall in unemployment of resources
items.markingKey: Using idle resources; actual growth.

items.stem: In a revision note Tariq wrote: ‘A rise in unemployment shifts the PPC inwards.’ Explain what is wrong with this claim.
items.answer: Unemployment means resources are idle, so the economy moves to a point inside the PPC; the PPC shifts only if the quantity or quality of resources changes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Unemployment means resources are idle, so the economy moves to a point inside the PPC; the PPC shifts only if the quantity or quality of resources changes. [2]

items.stem: Priya wrote in a homework answer: ‘Points beyond the PPC show the economy is producing very efficiently.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Points beyond the PPC are unattainable with current resources and technology.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Points beyond the PPC are unattainable with current resources and technology. [2]

items.stem: The table shows the maximum combinations of defence and public services that Marvona can produce. Combination: A, B, C, D, E; defence: 0, 10, 20, 30, 40; public services: 160, 150, 110, 60, 0. Marvona is currently producing 20 units of defence and 130 units of public services. Which describes this position?
options: Beyond the PPC: unattainable with current resources and technology
On the PPC: the economy is experiencing economic growth
On the PPC: resources fully and efficiently employed
Inside the PPC: some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently
items.answer: Beyond the PPC: unattainable with current resources and technology
items.markingKey: At 20 units of defence the maximum of public services is 110; 130 is more than this.

items.stem: The table shows the maximum combinations of consumer goods and capital goods that Loristan can produce. Combination: A, B, C, D, E; consumer goods: 0, 20, 40, 60, 80; capital goods: 340, 300, 220, 120, 0. Loristan is currently producing 60 units of consumer goods and 80 units of capital goods. (a) Explain whether this output is efficient. (b) Calculate the extra capital goods that could be produced without giving up any consumer goods. (c) Explain one reason why an economy might be at this point.
items.answer: (a) Inside the PPC: some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently. (b) 40 units. (c) Unemployment, e.g. a recession, or inefficient use of resources.
items.markingKey: (a) compare with maximum 120 [1]; conclusion [1] (b) 120 − 80 = 40 [1] (c) reason [1] [4]

items.stem: Extract: During a recession unemployment in Dravonia rose from 4% to 9%. The government responded with a programme to build new ports and railways, raising investment to 18% of GDP. Critics argue that the programme diverts resources away from consumer goods. At the same time a drought reduced the area of farmland that could be used. (a) Calculate the change in unemployment in percentage points. (b) Using a PPC, explain how the recession would be shown. (c) Explain the effect of the drought on the PPC.
items.answer: (a) 5 percentage points (b) A movement to a point inside the PPC: resources idle, capacity unchanged. (c) Loss of land reduces capacity (especially for food) so the PPC shifts or pivots inwards.
items.markingKey: (a) 9 − 4 [1] (b) Credit: A movement to a point inside the PPC: resources idle, capacity unchanged. [2] (c) Credit: Loss of land reduces capacity (especially for food) so the PPC shifts or pivots inwards. [2]

items.stem: An improvement in technology that only affects the production of good X causes the PPC to
options: pivot outwards along the X axis
items.answer: pivot outwards along the X axis
items.markingKey: Maximum X rises; maximum Y unchanged.

items.stem: In a revision note Kenji wrote: ‘An improvement in technology for producing cars shifts the whole PPC outwards in parallel.’ Identify what is wrong with this reasoning and give the correct explanation.
items.answer: If the technology only affects cars, the PPC pivots outwards along the car axis; the maximum output of the other good is unchanged.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – If the technology only affects cars, the PPC pivots outwards along the car axis; the maximum output of the other good is unchanged. [2]

items.stem: In a revision note Arjun wrote: ‘A fall in unemployment causes the PPC to shift outwards.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: A fall in unemployment moves the economy from inside towards the PPC; the PPC shifts only when capacity changes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – A fall in unemployment moves the economy from inside towards the PPC; the PPC shifts only when capacity changes. [2]

items.stem: Before a change, Esteria could produce a maximum of 80 units of agricultural goods or 240 units of industrial goods. After a new technology used only in producing agricultural goods, the maximum output of agricultural goods rose by 50% while the maximum output of industrial goods was unchanged. Calculate the new maximum output of agricultural goods.
items.answer: 120 units

items.stem: Before a change, Valdoria could produce a maximum of 150 units of consumer goods or 300 units of capital goods. After a rise in the size and skills of its labour force, the maximum output of consumer goods rose by 20% and that of capital goods by 20%. (a) Calculate the new maximum outputs of consumer goods and capital goods. (b) Describe how the PPC has changed. (c) Explain what happens to the opportunity cost of consumer goods in terms of capital goods (assume a straight-line PPC).
items.answer: (a) 180 consumer goods; 360 capital goods. (b) Parallel outward shift. (c) Before: 2 capital goods per consumer goods; after: 2: unchanged.
items.markingKey: (a) both maxima [2] (b) shift/pivot [1] (c) both opportunity costs and conclusion [2] [5]

items.stem: Extract: During a recession unemployment in Kestria rose from 6% to 13%. The government responded with a programme to build new ports and railways, raising investment to 18% of GDP. Critics argue that the programme diverts resources away from consumer goods. At the same time a drought reduced the area of farmland that could be used. (a) Using a PPC, explain how the recession would be shown. (b) Explain the opportunity cost of the investment programme once the economy returns to full employment. (c) Explain the effect of the drought on the PPC.
items.answer: (a) A movement to a point inside the PPC: resources idle, capacity unchanged. (b) Moving along the PPC: more capital goods means fewer consumer goods now. (c) Loss of land reduces capacity (especially for food) so the PPC shifts or pivots inwards.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: A movement to a point inside the PPC: resources idle, capacity unchanged. [2] (b) Credit: Moving along the PPC: more capital goods means fewer consumer goods now. [2] (c) Credit: Loss of land reduces capacity (especially for food) so the PPC shifts or pivots inwards. [2]
